[b]Emperor[/b]
King Henri dEstienne walked into the audience room of the Palais de liberté, a grand monument to the freedom of the Rosenmarkket state, a monument which had been built in challenge to the Montfleurois monarchy. He paused to stare up at the ceiling, which depicted the battle of Lagrange, the one that knocked Montfleur back from Rosenmarkke and effectively gave them independence.

He continued to walk, passing through the room towards the meeting chamber. It was funny, how history worked, because he was now the king of Montfleur and Rosenmarkket, the republican government having fallen under the strain of foreign ideology, namely the ideology of socialism. 

Entering the meeting room, he nodded to Thomas Lambeau, the man who had started the movement against the old government, and his president of state, Eleonore De Lorraine, the duchess of Lorraine.

I think began Henri, nodding, I think that moving the capital to this region was, a good call, he nodded, looking around the room which was panelled in oak and lacquer wainscotting, decorated with golden flourishes.

Trying to get the assembly to agree was like pulling teeth, I might as well become a dentist, replied Eleonore.

Please dont, replied Henri, We need you, he smiled, seating himself at the table, and placing a manila folder down.

I am displeased, however, there are still old socialist loyalists who seem intent on causing trouble, they see the new government, the provisional government, asilligitemate, said Henri.

Lambeau nodded, We expected this when we had our conference in early August, and signed the re-unification treaty, there really isnt much that can be done, 

Henri frowned, and then spoke, leaning back in his chair, We must built legitimacy, internally and externally, I am aware that December will see the right-wing Blue Union sweep the election, we will have the Rosenmarkke National Salvation Front aligned with our interests in the assembly, and a new governing framework is expected to be put into place following the election, 

Eleonore nodded, That is all correct, sir, and those will without a doubt quell any major issues, the biggest concern is financial, 

Yes, there is a major disparity between our two countries, which I believe can be addressed through the immediate introduction of a new deal, one which will incentivise the Estates to seek out their own welfare, replied the king.

Eleonore, But, the people of Rosenmarkke are used to the government being the source of welfare,

Henri laughed, And with what budget? 

Eleonore nodded, The one which will be passed in November, following the audits, right now we are treating both budgets as separate, but, the Rosenmarkket budget was horribly mismanaged, I mean most of it was going to the military, 

Henri nodded, Can we shift the budget? I mean, Charles Martel can he do so? 

I could request that of him, yes,he has no major constraints besides ensuring cohesion across all departments, replied Eleonore.

Lambeau, what is the situation with the estate legislatures? asked Henri.

They are finishing up their elections, regime loyalists there have all been shuffled out, replied Lambeau.

Excellent, because what I see, in terms of legitimacy, is that there is no symbol for people to grasp at, the joy of freedom is fading quickly as the tediousness of the state and normalcy returns, naturally people need a symbol, and I have a plan to ensure that symbol is unifying, stated Henri.

What do you plan? asked Eleonore.

It is an idea, which came to me by way of history, Marisalbia, are you familiar with it? asked Henri.

Eleonore nodded, Yes, the ancient empire from which Montfleur descends from and various other states on the White Sea.

That, that shall be our symbol, see the reunification has created a large state now on the East coast of Elseyr, and the entrance of the White Sea, a nation like ours hasnt been seen in centuries, history thus presents us with a unique opportunity, smiled Henri. 

Emperor, whispered Eleonore in a breathless whisper as she picked up on what Henri had laid down.

Emperor? asked Lambeau, Surely not, the imagery would be unprecedented, revolts would break out! 

Lambeau, intoned Henri calmly, The people see the Montfleurois crown as inevitable, this is merely another inevitability, and one which we shall frame as such to the grand assembly, in a week, when we meet with the dukes of the estates and the grand assembly, and we will push for a vote on that day, to ascend this nation,

[i][b]P I R N ─[/b][/i] More than a month has passed since the civil war erupted in Pirn, yet the situation shows little sign of easing for the [b]Union Government[/b]. Despite being outmatched and bogged down, the rebel faction, the [b]Republic Restoration Front (RPF)[/b], has remained firmly entrenched through guerrilla tactics in contested regions. Civilian casualties continue to rise, and the entirety of Rupert Region has almost fallen under rebel control, with 83% now occupied. Other areas, however, remain under the authority of the [b]Pirn Defence Force (PDF)[/b] and pro-Union spontaneous militia groups.

Prime Minister [i]Monica Franklin[/i] has yet to issue any further statements, but rumors are beginning to circulate that internal tensions are mounting. Critics point not only to the failure of the [i][b]Swift Strike, Swift Victory[/b][/i] campaign to end the conflict quickly, but also to the increasing civilian death toll, factors that have eroded public trust in the newly established Union Government within several loyalist regions. A growing number of citizens are voicing support for restoring the republic. Meanwhile, President [i]Ariana Doolan[/i] continues her efforts to steer public opinion, though her statements appear to be losing influence.

▌[i]I fear this civil war will bring down the Union Government if it drags on any longer. Pirn was clearly never prepared for a situation like this,[/i] [i]Ferdinand Lee[/i], spokesperson for the [b]Office of the President[/b], told the media.

The fighting remains particularly fierce in Rupert Region, currently the epicenter of the conflict. Although the Union Government and the PDF still hold a military advantage, the prolonged clashes have badly affected troop morale. In areas under RPF control, frustration is growing as civilians complain that the Union not only failed to evacuate them but is allowing the war to continue indefinitely. Some have openly shifted their support to the rebels, while others still wait, hoping for deliverance from the Union Government and the prime minister.
